The same patches are included for Gazpacho (2026.1), whose images will be published with the upcoming OSISM 11 release.

Keystone is a core service of every OSISM deployment, and all delegation mechanisms involved are available by default: Application credentials can be created by every user for their own projects. They are the recommended way to give automation access to the cloud and are widely used. EC2 credentials are used to access the S3 API of Ceph RGW or Swift with Keystone identities. Every user can create them. OAuth1 is part of Keystone's default [auth] methods (external,password,token,oauth1,mapped,application_credential), which OSISM does not change. Kolla only replaces the list when Keystone federation is enabled (password,token,openid,application_credential), which removes OAuth1 but leaves the other paths open. Trusts are created on behalf of users by services such as Heat and Magnum, and every user can create them. The token authentication method and [token] allow_rescope_scoped_token = True are Keystone defaults that OSISM does not change. Exploitation requires an attacker to hold a delegated credential of a victim — a leaked application credential, an EC2 access/secret key pair, or an OAuth1 access token — or a user to deliberately abuse their own narrow delegation. In both cases the attacker gains more than the delegation was meant to grant: persistent credentials that survive revocation of the original one, trusts carrying roles the delegation never had, and tokens for other projects of the credential owner.

Check the Running Keystone Version​ docker exec keystone pip show keystone | grep ^Version Because no fixed Keystone release exists upstream yet, your deployment is affected unless you have deployed an OSISM container image that includes the patches (see Remediation). Check Whether the Patched Image Is Deployed​ The fix introduces the module keystone.api._shared.delegation, which only exists in patched images: docker exec keystone /var/lib/kolla/venv/bin/python3 -c "import keystone.api._shared.delegation" \ 2>/dev/null && echo patched || echo vulnerable vulnerable means the running image does not contain the fix.
documents.s: How to Check if You Are Affected

documents.t: Keystone distinguishes primary authentication methods, which authenticate a user directly (password, token, totp, mapped, saml2, openid, external, kerberos, x509), from delegated credentials, which are deliberately narrow grants derived from a user (application_credential, ec2credential, oauth1, and trust-scoped tokens). API endpoints that mint a new, independent grant must reject delegated tokens, otherwise a narrow grant can bootstrap a broader or longer-lived one. Before the fix these guards were implemented separately per endpoint, and each of them recognized only some of the delegated methods.

_check_application_credential() in keystone/api/trusts.py only blocked tokens whose methods included application_credential. Tokens derived from an OAuth1 access token or an EC2 credential could create, list, read, and delete trusts. Since trust creation validates the requested roles against the trustor's full role assignments rather than against the roles of the requesting token, such a token could also delegate roles the delegation was never scoped to. _block_delegated_token_app_creds() in keystone/api/users.py only checked for a trust_id or an OAuth1 access_token_id on the token, so an EC2-derived token — which carries neither — could create and manage application credentials and access rules. PUT /v3/OS-OAUTH1/authorize/{request_token_id} in keystone/api/os_oauth1.py only rejected trust-scoped, OAuth1-scoped, and application credential tokens, so an EC2-derived token could authorize OAuth1 request tokens and thereby mint new OAuth1 access tokens. All three grants outlive the credential used to create them: revoking a leaked EC2 key pair or OAuth1 access token does not remove the trusts, application credentials, or access tokens it bootstrapped. The fix introduces keystone/api/_shared/delegation.py with a deny-by-default allowlist of primary authentication methods. is_delegated_method() treats every token whose methods are not entirely primary — including an empty method list, which occurs for ec2credential tokens after a fernet round-trip — as delegated, and all three endpoints now use this shared check. Application credential tokens keep their documented behavior (the opt-in [security_compliance] allow_insecure_application_credential_trust_escalation for trust management and the unrestricted/restricted distinction for creating further application credentials); OAuth1 and EC2 credentials are blocked unconditionally.
documents.s: Bug #2153453 — Delegated tokens can create persistent delegations

documents.t: token_authenticate() in keystone/auth/plugins/token.py implements the token authentication method, i.e. exchanging an existing token for a new one. Trust-scoped and OAuth1-scoped tokens were rejected unconditionally, but application credential tokens were only rejected when an explicit scope was requested: with the scope omitted, the request fell through to Keystone's default-project scoping and returned a token for the credential owner's default project — a different project than the one the application credential was bound to. EC2-derived tokens matched none of the checks and, with the default [token] allow_rescope_scoped_token = True, could be rescoped to any project the underlying user has a role in. The fix rejects every delegated token from the token authentication method using the same shared classification and returns HTTP 403.
documents.s: Bug #2158538 — Delegated tokens escape their project scope via token reauthentication

documents.t: The upstream fix consists of two changes that are interdependent and must be applied together; OSISM ships both in the patched images: trusts, oauth1, app-creds: reject delegated tokens across all endpoints (Bug #2153453) — introduces the shared delegation classification and the new [auth] additional_primary_auth_methods option and applies the check to trusts, application credentials, and OAuth1 authorization. auth: reject delegated tokens from token-method reauthentication (Bug #2158538) — applies the classification to the token authentication method and depends on the first change. warning Behavior changes after the fix: Any authentication method that is not built into Keystone is treated as a delegated credential and rejected from managing trusts, application credentials, and OAuth1 access tokens, and from token reauthentication. Deployments running a custom or third-party authentication plugin must list its method name in [auth] additional_primary_auth_methods, otherwise these workflows fail for users authenticated through it. Exchanging an application credential token or an EC2-derived token for a new token via the token authentication method is rejected with HTTP 403. Clients must authenticate with the application credential directly instead.

Besides the two upstream patches, the patched OSISM images for 2024.2, 2025.1, 2025.2, and 2026.1 contain the upstream change Ban ec2credential tokens from Keystone API, which is merged on master; its backports to the stable branches are proposed but not merged upstream. It rejects tokens derived from EC2 credentials for every Keystone API call except token validation and re-authentication, closing the whole class of EC2 token issues at the API boundary. The behavior is controlled by the new option [auth] ban_ec2credential_tokens (default True). Deployments that use EC2-derived tokens directly against the Keystone API must set it to False. The 2024.1 images contain only the two patches of the upstream fix, not this additional change.
documents.s: Additional Hardening in the OSISM Images

documents.t: Because no fixed Keystone release is available upstream, OSISM provides the fix as downstream patches for the Keystone container images via the following changes: container-images-kolla commit 01ae42c (PR #776) — patches for 2025.1 (Epoxy), 2025.2 (Flamingo), and 2026.1 (Gazpacho) container-images-kolla commit 59fa2a2 (PR #778) — community-curated backport for 2024.1 (Caracal) container-images-kolla commit 2c082f0 (PR #782) — community-curated backport for 2024.2 (Dalmatian) Patched rolling images are available for 2024.1, 2024.2, 2025.1, and 2025.2. A fix will be included in upcoming OSISM releases that ship the patched Keystone container images. Consult the OSISM Release Notes for version information and availability. The affected code runs in the Keystone API service (keystone container). Using rolling tags, override the Keystone container images in environments/kolla/images.yml. With a stable OSISM release the Kolla images are pulled from the kolla/release/<openstack_version> namespace with pinned version tags (docker_namespace in environments/kolla/configuration.yml), whereas the rolling images live in the kolla namespace. The image parameters therefore have to be overridden together with the tag; the tag override alone would point at an image that does not exist: environments/kolla/images.yml keystone_tag: "2024.1" # or "2024.2", "2025.1", "2025.2", depending on your OpenStack release keystone_image: "registry.osism.tech/kolla/keystone" keystone_fernet_image: "registry.osism.tech/kolla/keystone-fernet" keystone_ssh_image: "registry.osism.tech/kolla/keystone-ssh" Replace registry.osism.tech if you pull the images from a mirror. From 2025.2 on the Keystone role additionally runs an httpd container (keystone_httpd_image, keystone_httpd_tag) that contains no Keystone code; its tag follows keystone_tag by default, so pin keystone_httpd_tag to the currently deployed tag when overriding keystone_tag.

Because all deployments are affected and the vulnerabilities require only a delegated credential, applying the patched container image is the only complete remediation. Until the fix is deployed, consider the following measures: Disabling the rescoping of scoped tokens closes the token reauthentication path (Bug #2158538). Add the following to the configuration repository and redeploy Keystone: environments/kolla/files/overlays/keystone.conf [token] allow_rescope_scoped_token = False This also prevents legitimate clients from exchanging a scoped token for another scoped token; authenticating with an unscoped token or with credentials directly is not affected. It does not mitigate Bug #2153453. Auditing existing delegations. Trusts, application credentials, EC2 credentials, and OAuth1 access tokens that were created through a delegated token before the fix remain valid after it is applied and have to be revoked manually: openstack --os-cloud admin trust list openstack --os-cloud admin credential list --type ec2 openstack --os-cloud admin consumer list openstack --os-cloud admin application credential list --user <user> Application credentials can only be listed per user. Trusts whose trustee is not a service user, and credentials or consumers nobody can account for, are candidates for removal. Rotating EC2 credentials and OAuth1 access tokens that may have leaked. Rotating them is not enough on its own: trusts, application credentials, and OAuth1 access tokens that were created with such a credential before the rotation stay valid and have to be removed as described in point 2. Monitoring the Keystone API logs for POST /v3/OS-TRUST/trusts, POST /v3/users/{user_id}/application_credentials, and PUT /v3/OS-OAUTH1/authorize requests from unexpected sources.

documents.s: OSSA-2026-038: Multiple SSRF vulnerabilities in Glance web-download and HTTP image APIs

documents.t: The web-download import method ships with insecure default filtering that permits authenticated users to fetch arbitrary internal URLs, including cloud metadata endpoints. The URI validator does not perform DNS resolution before applying host filters, enabling bypass via attacker-controlled domains and DNS rebinding attacks. The HTTP image location API lacks host filtering entirely when the HTTP store is enabled, and fetched content is stored as image data accessible for download, converting blind SSRF into full-read exfiltration. Every OSISM deployment running an unpatched Glance version and using the web-download import method or HTTP image location APIs (enabled by default) is affected. Upstream has not published a CVSS score for this issue. The severity rating above is OSISM's assessment: an attacker holding a delegated credential can turn it into persistent access that survives revocation of that credential, obtain roles beyond the delegation, and reach other projects of the credential owner.

The upstream advisory states the affected ranges as >=16.0.0 <30.2.1, >=31.0.0 <31.1.1, and >=32.0.0 <32.0.1, so the fixes are expected in Glance 30.2.1 (2025.1/Epoxy), 31.1.1 (2025.2/Flamingo) and 32.0.1 (2026.1/Gazpacho). At the time of this advisory there is no fixed Glance release available upstream for any series. The upstream fixes are still under review on OpenDev and have not merged yet. documents.s: OSSA-2026-039: HAProxy configuration injection leading to remote code execution in Octavia

documents.t: Chen YuXiang of the Institute of Computing Technology, Chinese Academy of Sciences reported input validation flaws in the Octavia load balancer API. The tls_ciphers field of listeners and pools and the redirect_url and redirect_prefix fields of L7 policies were written into the HAProxy configuration that Octavia generates for the amphora without rejecting control characters. An authenticated user who owns a load balancer served by the Amphora provider can embed newlines in these fields and thereby inject arbitrary HAProxy configuration directives. An independent reporter, "Rolix", subsequently demonstrated that the injection can be escalated to the execution of arbitrary commands as root on the provider-managed amphora. According to the upstream advisory this allows an attacker to disclose other tenants' TLS private keys and certificates and the deployment heartbeat key stored on the amphora, and to reach the control-plane network the amphora is attached to. The issue was reported to the OpenStack Vulnerability Management Team by Thomas Goirand of Infomaniak on behalf of the reporter. Only the Amphora provider driver is affected. Other provider drivers, such as the OVN provider, do not render tenant input into an HAProxy configuration. Upstream has not published a CVSS score for this issue. The severity rating above is OSISM's assessment: every project member who may create load balancers can gain root access to a virtual machine operated by the cloud provider and, from there, network access to the Octavia management network; exploitation requires valid credentials and a load balancer owned by the attacker. Every OSISM deployment that runs an unpatched Octavia version with the Amphora provider is affected. Octavia and the Amphora provider are enabled in the OSISM defaults.

All OSISM releases up to and including 10.2.0 are affected, for every OpenStack release they support: the Kolla images pinned by OSISM 10.2.0 were built on 2026-08-14, before the upstream fixes merged. The OSISM or Octavia version alone does not tell whether a deployment already runs patched images, for example via rolling tags; use Check Whether the Patched Image Is Deployed for that. The upstream advisory states the affected ranges as >=0.8.0 <16.1.0, ==17.0.0 and ==18.0.0. The fix is contained in Octavia 16.1.0 (2025.1/Epoxy), released on 2026-08-26. For 2025.2 (Flamingo) and 2026.1 (Gazpacho) only the versions 17.0.0 and 18.0.0 are released and both are vulnerable; the fixes are merged on the stable branches and the releases 17.0.1 and 18.0.1 are proposed but not published yet. The tls_ciphers fields were introduced in Octavia 6.0.0. Older releases within the affected range are vulnerable only through the L7 policy redirect_url and redirect_prefix fields. OpenStack Release Upstream Status Fix in OSISM Images Caracal (2024.1) Unmaintained — backport proposed, not yet merged Community-curated backport (PR #803) Dalmatian (2024.2) End of life since 2026-04-29, no fix Community-curated backport (PR #803) Epoxy (2025.1) Fixed in Octavia 16.1.0 Upstream fix via stable/2025.1 branch Flamingo (2025.2) Fix merged on stable/2025.2, release 17.0.1 proposed Upstream fix via stable/2025.2 branch Gazpacho (2026.1) Fix merged on stable/2026.1, release 18.0.1 proposed Upstream fix via stable/2026.1 branch Hibiscus (2026.2, dev) Fix merged on master Not shipped by OSISM yet Caracal (2024.1) is unmaintained and Dalmatian (2024.2) reached end of life on 2026-04-29 upstream; neither will receive an official fixed release. Backports of both patches have been proposed on the unmaintained/2024.1 branch but have not merged yet; the stable/2024.2 branch no longer exists. For these two releases OSISM provides the fix as community-curated backports, shipped as downstream patches in the Octavia container images; the patched images for 2024.1 and 2024.2 have been available since 2026-09-21. For Epoxy (2025.1), Flamingo (2025.2) and Gazpacho (2026.1) the container images build Octavia from the upstream stable branches, on which both fixes merged between 2026-08-24 and 2026-08-26. Rebuilt images include the fix without additional downstream patches; this applies to the rolling images built since then. Patched container images are available for all OpenStack releases OSISM builds images for.

Octavia is enabled in the OSISM defaults (enable_octavia: "yes"), and kolla-ansible always enables the Amphora provider (octavia_provider_drivers). With the OSISM default neutron_plugin_agent: "ovn" the OVN provider is enabled in addition, but amphora stays the provider that is used when a user does not request one explicitly. A default OSISM deployment is therefore affected. Exploitation requires an authenticated user who is allowed to create or update listeners, pools or L7 policies of a load balancer in their own project — the normal permission of every load balancer user. No administrative role is needed. The attacker does not need access to the Octavia management network; the injected configuration is delivered to the amphora by Octavia itself. The vulnerable code — the API validation and the rendering of the HAProxy configuration — runs in the Octavia control plane services, not in the amphora image. That a compromised amphora has to be replaced after the control plane was patched (see Remediation) is OSISM's own assessment of the affected code path.

warning The docker commands in this section must be run on the nodes that run the Octavia containers, not on the manager node, where they return no result or a wrong result. The openstack commands are run on the manager node. The Octavia services are not necessarily all on the same nodes. Their placement is defined by the inventory groups octavia-api, octavia-worker and octavia-health-manager. By default these are children of octavia, which in turn defaults to control. In production deployments with dedicated network nodes, octavia_worker and octavia_health_manager commonly run on the network nodes, while octavia_api runs on the control nodes. Check the inventory of the deployment for the members of these groups and run the commands on every node listed there. Check Whether Octavia Is Deployed​ On every node in the octavia-api, octavia-worker and octavia-health-manager groups: docker ps --format '{{.Names}}' | grep ^octavia No output on all of these nodes means Octavia is not deployed and the deployment is not affected. Check the Enabled Provider Drivers​ On a node in the octavia-api group (by default a control node): docker exec octavia_api grep enabled_provider_drivers /etc/octavia/octavia.conf If amphora is listed as an enabled provider driver, users can create vulnerable load balancers. On the manager node, list the existing load balancers served by amphorae: openstack --os-cloud admin loadbalancer list --provider amphora These are the load balancers whose amphorae may already have received an injected configuration. The list tells whether the deployment is exposed to existing tenant input at all, and it is the set of load balancers to audit and, if necessary, fail over after the update, as described in Remediation and Mitigation. Deployments without any load balancer on the Amphora provider are affected but have nothing to audit. Check the Running Octavia Version​ On a node in the octavia-api group (by default a control node): docker exec octavia_api pip show octavia | grep ^Version Versions below 16.1.0 as well as 17.0.0 and 18.0.0 are affected. Images built from a stable branch report a development version (for example 17.0.1.devN), which does not tell whether the fix is included — use the next check. Check Whether the Patched Image Is Deployed​ The fix introduces VALID_CIPHER_RE and INVALID_URL_CHARS_RE in octavia/common/validate.py, which only exist in patched images. Run this on every node in the octavia-api, octavia-worker and octavia-health-manager groups. The loop only checks the Octavia containers that actually run on the node, so a node that hosts only some of the services (for example a network node with the worker and health manager) does not produce false results for the others: for container in $(docker ps --format '{{.Names}}' | grep -E '^octavia_(api|worker|health_manager)$'); do docker exec $container /var/lib/kolla/venv/bin/python3 -c \ "from octavia.common import validate as v; v.VALID_CIPHER_RE; v.INVALID_URL_CHARS_RE" \ 2>/dev/null && echo "$container: patched" || echo "$container: vulnerable" done vulnerable means the running image does not contain both fixes. No output means none of the three containers runs on this node. Collect the results from all nodes: the deployment is only fixed when every octavia_api, octavia_worker and octavia_health_manager container reports patched.

documents.t: The Amphora provider renders the HAProxy configuration of a load balancer from a Jinja template in the Octavia control plane (JinjaTemplater in octavia/common/jinja/haproxy/combined_listeners/jinja_cfg.py) and uploads the result to the amphora. HAProxy configuration files are line-oriented: a value that contains a newline ends the directive it belongs to, and everything after it is parsed as additional directives or sections. Two groups of tenant-controlled fields reached the template without a check for such characters.

check_cipher_prohibit_list() in octavia/common/validate.py only split the cipher string of a listener or pool at : and compared the parts with the configured prohibit list; it did not restrict the characters of the string. _transform_listener() and _transform_pool() passed tls_ciphers unchanged to the template, where it ends up in the bind line of the frontend or the server lines of the backend. The fix adds check_cipher_string(), which the API now calls for every cipher string and which only accepts the characters used by OpenSSL cipher strings: VALID_CIPHER_RE = re.compile(r'^[A-Za-z0-9\-+!:@=_.]+\Z') In addition, _transform_listener() and _transform_pool() verify the value again when the configuration is generated. A value in the database that does not match is replaced with [api_settings] default_listener_ciphers or [api_settings] default_pool_ciphers, and a warning is logged.
documents.s: Bug #2162101 — Injection via the tls_ciphers field

documents.t: url() in octavia/common/validate.py validates redirect_url and redirect_prefix with the rfc3986 library. The library percent-encodes control characters before it validates the URL (a newline becomes %0A), so such URLs passed the structural checks. Octavia, however, stores the raw input, and _transform_l7policy() wrote it unencoded into the redirect location and redirect prefix lines of the HAProxy configuration. The fix rejects URLs that contain control characters or spaces before they are passed to rfc3986: INVALID_URL_CHARS_RE = re.compile(r'[\x00-\x20\x7f-\x9f]') The new _sanitize_url() in jinja_cfg.py applies the same expression when the configuration is generated and clears a redirect_url or redirect_prefix from the database that does not pass, logging a warning.
documents.s: Bug #2162103 — Injection via L7 policy redirect URLs

documents.t: Both issues were originally triaged upstream as a low-severity hardening opportunity, and the fixes were developed and merged in public. They were reclassified after a proof of concept showed that injected HAProxy directives can be used to execute arbitrary commands as root on the amphora. With root access to the amphora an attacker can read the TLS certificates and private keys and the heartbeat key stored there, and can use the amphora's interface in the Octavia management network to reach the control plane. This bug has no fix of its own: it is closed by the two changes above.
documents.s: Bug #2167565 — Escalation to remote code execution

documents.t: The upstream fix consists of two changes per branch that OSISM ships together in the patched images. The second change uses the imports and the logger that the first one adds to jinja_cfg.py, so they have to be applied in this order: Fix HAProxy config injection via tls_ciphers field (Bug #2162101) — validates the cipher strings of listeners and pools in the API and when the configuration is generated. Fix HAProxy config injection via L7 policy redirect URLs (Bug #2162103) — rejects control characters and spaces in redirect_url and redirect_prefix in the API and when the configuration is generated. warning Behavior changes after the fix: The API rejects tls_ciphers values that contain characters other than alphanumerics, -, +, !, :, @, =, _ and ., and redirect URLs that contain spaces or control characters, with a validation error. Invalid values that are already stored in the database are not removed. They are replaced with the default ciphers (tls_ciphers) or dropped (redirect_url, redirect_prefix) the next time the configuration of the load balancer is generated, which changes the behavior of the affected listener, pool or L7 policy.

Because 2024.1 (Caracal) and 2024.2 (Dalmatian) receive no fixed upstream release, OSISM provides the fix for these releases as downstream patches for the Octavia container images via the following change: container-images-kolla commit efaa873 (PR #803) — community-curated backport for 2024.1 (Caracal) and 2024.2 (Dalmatian); it also re-enables the build of the Octavia images for 2024.1 For 2025.1 (Epoxy), 2025.2 (Flamingo) and 2026.1 (Gazpacho) the container images build Octavia from the upstream stable branches, which contain the fix as of Octavia 16.1.0 and the upcoming 17.0.1 and 18.0.1. Rebuilt images include the fix automatically. Patched rolling images are available for 2024.1, 2024.2, 2025.1, 2025.2, and 2026.1. No OSISM release up to and including 10.2.0 ships the patched Octavia container images; on these releases the fix can only be obtained through the rolling tags as described below. A fix will be included in the next OSISM release. Consult the OSISM Release Notes for version information and availability. The affected code runs in the Octavia API service (input validation) and in the services that generate the HAProxy configuration (octavia_worker, and octavia_health_manager during failovers). Using rolling tags, override all Octavia container images in environments/kolla/images.yml. With a stable OSISM release the Kolla images are pulled from the kolla/release/<openstack_version> namespace with pinned version tags (docker_namespace in environments/kolla/configuration.yml), whereas the rolling images live in the kolla namespace. The image parameters therefore have to be overridden together with the tag; the tag override alone would point at an image that does not exist: environments/kolla/images.yml octavia_tag: "2024.1" # or "2024.2", "2025.1", "2025.2", "2026.1", depending on your OpenStack release octavia_api_image: "registry.osism.tech/kolla/octavia-api" octavia_driver_agent_image: "registry.osism.tech/kolla/octavia-driver-agent" octavia_health_manager_image: "registry.osism.tech/kolla/octavia-health-manager" octavia_housekeeping_image: "registry.osism.tech/kolla/octavia-housekeeping" octavia_worker_image: "registry.osism.tech/kolla/octavia-worker" Replace registry.osism.tech if you pull the images from a mirror. Verify the deployed images on every Octavia node with the check in Check Whether the Patched Image Is Deployed. The amphora image does not contain the affected code and does not need to be rebuilt for this issue. The OSISM defaults set octavia_amp_image_tag: amphora independently of octavia_tag, so the override above does not change which amphora image is used. Updating the control plane does not repair amphorae that already run an injected configuration. After the update, audit the existing load balancers as described below and fail over every load balancer with a suspicious value, which replaces its amphorae with new instances: openstack --os-cloud admin loadbalancer failover <loadbalancer>

The affected fields cannot be disabled by configuration, and the Octavia policies cannot restrict individual fields of a listener, pool or L7 policy. Applying the patched container images is the only effective remediation. Until the fix is deployed, and afterwards to detect earlier exploitation, consider the following measures: Auditing the existing listeners and pools for cipher strings with unexpected characters. Every line of output names a resource and its project that must be investigated: for type in listener pool; do for id in $(openstack --os-cloud admin loadbalancer $type list -f value -c id); do openstack --os-cloud admin loadbalancer $type show "$id" -f json | python3 -c ' import json, re, sys d = json.load(sys.stdin) if re.search(r"[^A-Za-z0-9\-+!:@=_.]", d.get("tls_ciphers") or ""): print(sys.argv[1], d["id"], d["project_id"])' $type done done Auditing the existing L7 policies for redirect URLs with spaces or control characters: for id in $(openstack --os-cloud admin loadbalancer l7policy list -f value -c id); do openstack --os-cloud admin loadbalancer l7policy show "$id" -f json | python3 -c ' import json, re, sys d = json.load(sys.stdin) for field in ("redirect_url", "redirect_prefix"): if re.search(r"[\x00-\x20\x7f-\x9f]", d.get(field) or ""): print("l7policy", d["id"], d["project_id"], field)' done Treating every hit as a potential compromise of the amphorae of that load balancer: fail over the load balancer once the patched images are deployed, replace the TLS certificates and private keys that were configured on it, and review the activity of the owning project. Monitoring the logs of octavia_worker and octavia_health_manager after the update for the messages has invalid tls_ciphers in DB, falling back to default and in DB, clearing. They are written when a stored value is neutralized and identify the affected listener, pool or L7 policy. Verifying that the security groups and firewall rules of the Octavia management network only allow the traffic Octavia needs between the amphorae and the control plane (the amphora agent port 9443/tcp towards the amphorae, the health manager port 5555/udp towards the control plane). This limits what an attacker can reach from a compromised amphora.

documents.s: OSSA-2026-045: Cross-project information disclosure in Cinder Messages API

documents.t: Yuliang Xiao, an independent reporter, and Chen YuXiang of the Institute of Computing Technology, Chinese Academy of Sciences independently reported that the "List messages" call of the Cinder Block Storage API (GET /v3/{project_id}/messages, available since API microversion 3.3) is not restricted to the project of the caller. A user with the member or reader role in any project receives the non-expired user messages of all projects. Cinder records a user message when an asynchronous operation on a volume, snapshot or backup fails, for example when the scheduler finds no backend for a new volume or an image cannot be copied to a volume. The response therefore discloses the UUIDs and types of resources owned by other projects, together with the request IDs, the timestamps and the text of these messages. The message texts are generic by design, and the response does not contain the project IDs of the other projects. Upstream has not published a CVSS score for this issue. The severity rating above is OSISM's assessment (CVSS 3.1 base score 4.3, AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:L/I:N/A:N): every project member or reader can exploit the issue with a single API call, but the disclosed information is limited to resource identifiers and generic status messages and does not grant access to the resources of other projects. Every OSISM deployment running an unpatched Cinder version is affected. Cinder is enabled in the OSISM defaults.

All OSISM releases up to and including 10.3.0 and 11.0.2 are affected. The Kolla images pinned by OSISM 10.3.0 (OpenStack 2025.1) and 11.0.2 (OpenStack 2026.1) were built on 2026-10-01 and 2026-10-19, before the fix was available. The OSISM or Cinder version alone does not tell whether a deployment already runs a patched image, for example via rolling tags; use Check Whether the Patched Image Is Deployed for that. The upstream advisory states the affected ranges as >=9.0.0 <26.3.1, ==27.0.0, ==28.0.0 and ==29.0.0, so the fix for 2025.1 (Epoxy) is expected in Cinder 26.3.1. For 2025.2 (Flamingo), 2026.1 (Gazpacho) and 2026.2 (Hibiscus) only the versions 27.0.0, 28.0.0 and 29.0.0 are released, and all three are vulnerable; the fixes are expected in the next point release of each series. The user messages API first appeared in Cinder 9.0.0 (Newton), so every series since then is affected, including 2024.1 (Caracal) and 2024.2 (Dalmatian). At the time of this advisory there is no fixed Cinder release available upstream for any series. The upstream fixes are still under review on OpenDev and have not merged yet. OpenStack Release Upstream Status Fix in OSISM Images Caracal (2024.1) Unmaintained, no upstream fix Community-curated backport (PR #820) Dalmatian (2024.2) End of life since 2026-04-29, no fix Community-curated backport (PR #820) Epoxy (2025.1) Vulnerable — fix proposed (26.3.1), not yet merged Proposed upstream patch (PR #820) Flamingo (2025.2) Vulnerable — fix proposed, not yet merged Proposed upstream patch (PR #820) Gazpacho (2026.1) Vulnerable — fix proposed, not yet merged Proposed upstream patch (PR #820) Hibiscus (2026.2) Vulnerable — fix proposed, not yet merged Not shipped by OSISM yet Indri (2027.1, dev) Fix proposed on master, not yet merged Not shipped by OSISM yet Caracal (2024.1) is unmaintained and Dalmatian (2024.2) reached end of life on 2026-04-29 upstream; neither will receive an official fixed release, and no upstream backport has been proposed for these branches. For these two releases OSISM provides the fix as a community-curated backport of the 2025.1 patch, shipped as a downstream patch in the Cinder container images. For Epoxy (2025.1), Flamingo (2025.2) and Gazpacho (2026.1) the OSISM container images carry the proposed upstream patch ahead of its official upstream release. Patched container images are available for all OpenStack releases OSISM builds images for.

Cinder is enabled in the OSISM defaults (enable_cinder: "yes"); only deployments that set enable_cinder: "no" in environments/kolla/configuration.yml do not run it. The user messages API is always part of the Cinder API; there is no option to disable it. The list call is governed by the policy message:get_all, which by default admits every user with the reader or member role in a project, and OSISM does not override this policy. A default OSISM deployment is therefore affected. Exploitation requires nothing but a token for a project in which the attacker holds one of these roles; neither an administrative role nor a particular configuration is needed. The response contains every message that has not been removed yet. Messages expire after [DEFAULT] message_ttl (default 30 days) and are deleted by a periodic task of cinder-scheduler every [DEFAULT] message_reap_interval (default 24 hours); neither OSISM nor kolla-ansible changes these options. How much is exposed therefore depends on how many operations of other projects failed during that period. The disclosed resource UUIDs do not grant access to the resources themselves, and because the response contains no project IDs, attributing a resource to a project requires a separate source of information. The vulnerable code path runs only in the Cinder API service (cinder_api container). The cinder-scheduler, cinder-volume and cinder-backup services create user messages but never list them. That only the cinder-api image has to be updated is OSISM's own assessment of the affected code path.

Run the docker commands on every node of the cinder-api inventory group (by default the control nodes) and the openstack command on the manager node. Check Whether Cinder Is Deployed​ docker ps --format '{{.Names}}' | grep ^cinder_api No output on all nodes of the cinder-api group means the Cinder API is not deployed and the deployment is not affected. Check the Running Cinder Version​ docker exec cinder_api pip show cinder | grep ^Version Because no fixed Cinder release exists upstream yet, your deployment is affected unless you have deployed an OSISM container image that includes the patch (see Remediation). Images built from a stable branch report a development version such as 26.3.1.dev1 (2025.1) or 28.0.1.dev11 (2026.1), and the release tags of the images pinned by OSISM 10.3.0 and 11.0.2 carry the number of the next point release in their name (26.3.1.20261001, 28.0.1.20261019). Neither means that the fix is included; use the next check. Check Whether the Patched Image Is Deployed​ The fix changes the default of the project_only parameter of _messages_get_query() from False to True: docker exec cinder_api /var/lib/kolla/venv/bin/python3 -c \ "import inspect; from cinder.db.sqlalchemy import api; \ print(inspect.signature(api._messages_get_query).parameters['project_only'].default)" True means the running image contains the fix, False means it is vulnerable. The deployment is only fixed when the check prints True on every node of the cinder-api group. Check Which User Messages Are Exposed​ openstack --os-cloud admin --os-volume-api-version 3.3 volume message list An administrator sees the messages of all projects. On an unpatched deployment every user with the member or reader role in any project sees the same list. An empty list means that nothing is exposed at the moment; new messages are created whenever an asynchronous operation fails.

documents.t: The user messages API is implemented by MessagesController in cinder/api/v3/messages.py. The "Show message" and "Delete message" calls load a single message through message_get(), which queries the database in _message_get() with project_only="yes", so a regular user only finds the messages of their own project. These two calls are not affected. MessagesController.index(), which implements the "List messages" call, authorizes the policy message:get_all without a target object. context.authorize() then checks the policy against the caller's own project, which every user with the reader or member role in that project passes. The request parameters are handed on through API.get_all() in cinder/message/api.py to message_get_all() in cinder/db/sqlalchemy/api.py, which builds its query with _generate_paginate_query() and the query helper registered for messages in PAGINATION_HELPERS, _messages_get_query(): def _messages_get_query(context, project_only=False): return model_query(context, models.Message, project_only=project_only) model_query() only restricts a query to the caller's project when project_only is set and the request comes from a regular user (is_user_context()). Because _generate_paginate_query() calls the helper without further arguments, the default project_only=False applied, no project filter was added, and the list contained the messages of all projects. The fix changes the default to project_only=True: def _messages_get_query(context, project_only=True): return model_query(context, models.Message, project_only=project_only) Regular users now only receive the messages of their own project. Administrators keep seeing the messages of all projects, because model_query() does not apply the project filter to admin contexts. On 2026.1 and older releases the function is located in cinder/db/sqlalchemy/api.py, on 2026.2 and master in cinder/db/api.py. The fix also adds unit tests which verify that message_get_all() and message_get() only return messages of the caller's project. It introduces no configuration options and no API changes; the only visible change is that regular users no longer see the messages of other projects.

Because no fixed Cinder release is available upstream, OSISM provides the fix as downstream patches for the Cinder container images via the following change: container-images-kolla commit b56b799 (PR #820) — the proposed upstream patches for 2025.1 (Epoxy), 2025.2 (Flamingo) and 2026.1 (Gazpacho), and a community-curated backport of the 2025.1 patch for 2024.1 (Caracal) and 2024.2 (Dalmatian); it also re-enables the build of the Cinder images for 2024.1 Patched rolling images are available for 2024.1, 2024.2, 2025.1, 2025.2, and 2026.1. No OSISM release up to and including 10.3.0 and 11.0.2 ships the patched Cinder container images; on these releases the fix can only be obtained through the rolling tags as described below. A fix will be included in upcoming OSISM releases that ship the patched Cinder container images. Consult the OSISM Release Notes for version information and availability. The vulnerable code path runs in the Cinder API service (cinder_api container), so it is sufficient to update the cinder-api container image. Using rolling tags, override it in environments/kolla/images.yml. With a stable OSISM release the Kolla images are pulled from the kolla/release/<openstack_version> namespace with pinned version tags (docker_namespace in environments/kolla/configuration.yml), whereas the rolling images live in the kolla namespace. The image parameter therefore has to be overridden together with the tag; the tag override alone would point at an image that does not exist: environments/kolla/images.yml cinder_api_tag: "2024.1" # or "2024.2", "2025.1", "2025.2", "2026.1", depending on your OpenStack release cinder_api_image: "registry.osism.tech/kolla/cinder-api" Replace registry.osism.tech if you pull the images from a mirror. Verify the deployed image on every node of the cinder-api group with the check in Check Whether the Patched Image Is Deployed. The cinder-scheduler, cinder-volume and cinder-backup images contain the same code but never run the message list query; they do not need to be updated for this issue.

Every OSISM deployment that runs Cinder is affected, and the vulnerable call is available to every project member and reader. Applying the patched container image is the only complete remediation. Until it is deployed, consider the following measures: Restricting the list call to administrators through a policy override. Add the following to environments/kolla/files/overlays/cinder/policy.yaml in the configuration repository (create the file if it does not exist) and apply it with osism apply -a reconfigure cinder: environments/kolla/files/overlays/cinder/policy.yaml "message:get_all": "rule:context_is_admin" This closes the vulnerable code path completely. It also removes the message list for regular users: openstack volume message list fails for them, and the Messages tabs of volumes, snapshots and backups in Horizon can no longer retrieve messages. Showing or deleting a message by its ID keeps working. Remove the override once the patched image is deployed. Monitoring the Cinder API logs for list calls. The Cinder API logs every request together with the user and project ID of the caller: docker exec cinder_api grep -E 'GET [^ ]+/messages([?][^ ]*)?$' /var/log/kolla/cinder/cinder-api.log Before the fix, a list call of a regular user without a resource_uuid filter returned the messages of all projects. Calls with a resource_uuid filter, as Horizon sends them for the Messages tab of a volume, snapshot or backup, only return the messages of that resource. With central logging, which is enabled in the OSISM defaults, search for these requests in OpenSearch to cover the whole retention period.

documents.s: OSSA-2026-050: keystonemiddleware access rules bypass via X-Service-Token

documents.t: Nassim Abbaoui of OVHcloud reported that the auth_token middleware of keystonemiddleware skips the enforcement of application credential access rules as soon as a request carries an X-Service-Token header, regardless of whether that service token is valid. Access rules restrict an application credential to individual API calls (service, method and path). Anyone holding an access-restricted application credential can bypass these restrictions by adding an X-Service-Token header to the request; depending on the service, the header has to contain a valid token, such as a token of the same credential, or any value at all. The credential then acts with the full role-based permissions of the user who created it in every OpenStack API that uses the auth_token middleware. The same check also skipped token binding ([keystone_authtoken] enforce_token_bind, for example Kerberos) when delay_auth_decision is enabled. OSISM does not use token binding. The CVE record rates the issue with a CVSS 3.1 base score of 8.3 (AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:L). Only deployments in which application credentials with access rules are in use are affected.

The upstream advisory states the affected ranges as <10.9.2, >=10.10.0 <10.12.2, >=11.0.0 <12.0.1 and >=13.0.0 <13.0.2. The fixed upstream releases are keystonemiddleware 10.9.2 for 2025.1 (Epoxy), 10.13.0 for 2025.2 (Flamingo), 12.1.0 for 2026.1 (Gazpacho) and 13.0.2 for 2026.2 (Hibiscus). The versions 10.12.2 and 12.0.1, which the ranges imply, have not been released. All OSISM releases up to and including 10.3.0 and 11.0.2 are affected. The Kolla images pinned by these releases contain keystonemiddleware 10.12.1 (OpenStack 2025.1) and 12.0.0 (OpenStack 2026.1). Use Check the Running keystonemiddleware Version to find out whether a deployment already runs a fixed version, for example via rolling tags. OpenStack Release Upstream Status Fix in OSISM Images Caracal (2024.1) Unmaintained, no upstream fix keystonemiddleware 10.9.2 pinned (PR #828) Dalmatian (2024.2) End of life since 2026-04-29, no fix keystonemiddleware 10.13.0 pinned (PR #828) Epoxy (2025.1) Fixed in keystonemiddleware 10.9.2 Upstream fix via stable/2025.1 upper constraints (PR #831) Flamingo (2025.2) Fixed in keystonemiddleware 10.13.0 Upstream fix via stable/2025.2 upper constraints Gazpacho (2026.1) Fixed in keystonemiddleware 12.1.0 Upstream fix via stable/2026.1 upper constraints Hibiscus (2026.2) Fixed in keystonemiddleware 13.0.2 Not shipped by OSISM yet Indri (2027.1, dev) Fix merged on master Not shipped by OSISM yet The Kolla images install keystonemiddleware from PyPI at the version pinned in the upper constraints of the OpenStack requirements project. For 2025.1 (Epoxy), 2025.2 (Flamingo) and 2026.1 (Gazpacho) upstream has raised these constraints to the fixed releases; rebuilt images include the fix without additional downstream patches. Caracal (2024.1) is unmaintained and Dalmatian (2024.2) reached end of life on 2026-04-29 upstream; neither will receive an official fixed release. For these two releases OSISM pins a fixed keystonemiddleware release of a newer series in the upper constraints: 10.9.2 (2025.1 line) for 2024.1 and 10.13.0 (2025.2 line) for 2024.2. Both releases also contain the fix for OSSA-2026-001. Patched container images are available for all OpenStack releases OSISM builds images for; the patched rolling images have been available since 2026-11-03.

keystonemiddleware is a library. Its auth_token middleware validates the tokens of incoming requests in the API services of every OpenStack project except Keystone itself. In a default OSISM deployment these are Nova, Neutron, Glance, Placement, Cinder, Designate and Octavia; further API services such as Barbican, Manila, Ironic, Magnum, Aodh or Gnocchi are affected as well when they are enabled. Application credentials with access rules are not created by OSISM or kolla-ansible. They are created by users, who are allowed to do so under the default Keystone policies. A deployment is therefore affected as soon as a user restricts an application credential with access rules and hands it to a party that should only be able to make the permitted calls, for example a CI system or a monitoring agent. That party can then use the credential with the full permissions of its owner. Application credentials without access rules and regular user tokens are not affected. kolla-ansible does not set service_token_roles_required for Nova, Neutron, Glance, Placement and Octavia, so these API services accept any valid token as a service token and are exploitable; the Glance API additionally runs with delay_auth_decision = true (see Vulnerability Details). Cinder and Designate set service_token_roles_required = true, which blocks the bypass for users without a service role. That Cinder and Designate are not exploitable in a default OSISM deployment is OSISM's own assessment of the affected code path; update their images nevertheless.

Run the docker commands on every node that runs OpenStack API services (by default the control nodes). Check Whether Application Credentials With Access Rules Exist​ On a node of the mariadb group, enter the MariaDB root password (database_password in environments/kolla/secrets.yml) when prompted: docker exec -it mariadb mariadb -uroot -p -N -B -e \ 'SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT application_credential_id) FROM keystone.application_credential_access_rule;' 0 means that no application credential with access rules exists at the moment and the issue cannot be exploited. Users can create such credentials at any time, so update the images anyway. Check the Running keystonemiddleware Version​ for c in $(docker ps --format '{{.Names}}' | grep -E '(_api|_api_cfn|^neutron_server|^swift_proxy_server)$'); do echo -n "$c: "; docker exec "$c" pip show keystonemiddleware | grep ^Version done Compare each version with the affected ranges above. 10.9.2, 10.13.0, 12.1.0 and 13.0.2 are fixed; 10.12.1 and 12.0.0, which the images of OSISM 10.3.0 and 11.0.2 contain, are vulnerable. The deployment is only fixed when every API container on every node reports a fixed version.

documents.t: BaseAuthProtocol.validate_allowed_request() in keystonemiddleware/auth_token/__init__.py checks the request against the access rules of the application credential in the user token. A request that carries a service token is part of a chain of service-to-service calls (for example Nova calling Cinder on behalf of a user) and is therefore exempt from the access rules. The function tested only for the presence of the X-Service-Token header, not for the result of its validation: if request.service_token: return How the bypass is exploited depends on the configuration of the service: With [keystone_authtoken] service_token_roles_required = False, the upstream default before the fix, the middleware accepts any valid token as a service token. The attacker sends a token issued for the restricted application credential in both X-Auth-Token and X-Service-Token; both tokens are valid, the access rules are skipped, and the request is accepted. With delay_auth_decision enabled, as in the Glance API, an invalid service token does not lead to a rejection; the request continues as a regular user request. Any value in X-Service-Token is sufficient. With service_token_roles_required = True and delay_auth_decision disabled, the middleware rejects the request with 401 because the service token is not valid, unless the attacker also holds a token with one of the roles in [keystone_authtoken] service_token_roles. The same presence test decided whether _confirm_token_bind() runs, so a service token also skipped token binding. The fix requires a validated service token in both places: if request.service_token and request.service_token_valid: return Because a valid token is still accepted as a service token while service_token_roles_required = False, the fixed releases also change the default of this option to True. Only then is a token without a service role rejected as service token, and the access rules are enforced.

The upstream fix consists of two changes per stable series, which the fixed releases ship together: Change service_token_roles_required default config — sets [keystone_authtoken] service_token_roles_required to True, so that a token in X-Service-Token is only accepted as a service token when its user holds one of the roles in [keystone_authtoken] service_token_roles (default: service). On master and 2026.2 this default was already in place before the fix; keystonemiddleware 13.0.0 contains it. Fix service-token presence bypass of access_rules and token bind (Bug #2162748) — requires a valid service token before skipping the access rules or the token binding check. warning The new default service_token_roles_required = True makes OpenStack services reject service tokens whose user does not hold a role from service_token_roles. In kolla-ansible only Nova sends service tokens ([service_user] send_service_user_token = true), and its service user nova is granted the service role in the service project. Blazar, Cinder, Designate, Masakari and Watcher already set service_token_roles_required = true explicitly. Default OSISM deployments are therefore not expected to change behavior. Deployments that send service tokens as a user without the service role, for example through configuration overlays, receive 401 responses on these inter-service requests after the update. Do not set service_token_roles_required = false to work around this: it reopens the bypass.

The Kolla images install keystonemiddleware at the version pinned in the upper constraints. OSISM pinned the fixed releases for all OpenStack releases it builds images for with the following change: container-images-kolla commit 147fb67 (PR #828) — pins keystonemiddleware 10.9.2 for 2024.1, 10.13.0 for 2024.2, 2025.1 and 2025.2, and 12.1.0 for 2026.1 After upstream raised the upper constraints of 2025.1, 2025.2 and 2026.1 to the fixed releases, the OSISM pins for these three releases were removed again: container-images-kolla commit aea4cc3 (PR #831) — the images of 2025.1 now contain keystonemiddleware 10.9.2 from the upstream constraints instead of 10.13.0; 2025.2 and 2026.1 keep 10.13.0 and 12.1.0 Patched rolling images are available for 2024.1, 2024.2, 2025.1, 2025.2, and 2026.1. No OSISM release up to and including 10.3.0 and 11.0.2 ships the patched container images; on these releases the fix can only be obtained through the rolling tags as described below. A fix will be included in upcoming OSISM releases that ship the patched container images. Consult the OSISM Release Notes for version information and availability. The vulnerable code runs in the API service of every OpenStack project that uses the auth_token middleware, so the API images of all enabled services have to be updated. Using rolling tags, override them in environments/kolla/images.yml. With a stable OSISM release the Kolla images are pulled from the kolla/release/<openstack_version> namespace with pinned version tags (docker_namespace in environments/kolla/configuration.yml), whereas the rolling images live in the kolla namespace. The image parameters therefore have to be overridden together with the tags; the tag override alone would point at images that do not exist. The following covers the API services of a default OSISM deployment: environments/kolla/images.yml nova_api_tag: "2025.1" # or "2024.1", "2024.2", "2025.2", "2026.1", depending on your OpenStack release nova_api_image: "registry.osism.tech/kolla/nova-api" neutron_server_tag: "2025.1" neutron_server_image: "registry.osism.tech/kolla/neutron-server" glance_api_tag: "2025.1" glance_api_image: "registry.osism.tech/kolla/glance-api" placement_api_tag: "2025.1" placement_api_image: "registry.osism.tech/kolla/placement-api" cinder_api_tag: "2025.1" cinder_api_image: "registry.osism.tech/kolla/cinder-api" designate_api_tag: "2025.1" designate_api_image: "registry.osism.tech/kolla/designate-api" octavia_api_tag: "2025.1" octavia_api_image: "registry.osism.tech/kolla/octavia-api" Add the *_api_tag and *_api_image parameters of every further API service you have enabled in the same way, for example barbican_api_tag and barbican_api_image with the image registry.osism.tech/kolla/barbican-api. Replace registry.osism.tech if you pull the images from a mirror. Commit the override to the configuration repository and roll it out: osism apply configuration osism apply -a pull nova osism apply nova osism apply -a pull neutron osism apply neutron osism apply -a pull glance osism apply glance osism apply -a pull placement osism apply placement osism apply -a pull cinder osism apply cinder osism apply -a pull designate osism apply designate osism apply -a pull octavia osism apply octavia See Security Updates for the individual steps, how to verify the deployed image, and when to remove the override again. The other images of these services (for example nova-conductor, neutron-metadata-agent or cinder-volume) contain keystonemiddleware as well but do not run the auth_token middleware; they do not need to be updated for this issue. Keystone does not use the auth_token middleware.

Deployments without application credentials that carry access rules (see Check Whether Application Credentials With Access Rules Exist) cannot be exploited at the moment; updating the images at the next regular maintenance is sufficient. Otherwise, applying the patched container images is the only complete remediation. Until they are deployed, consider the following measures: Reviewing which application credentials carry access rules and who holds them. List the affected credentials and their owners on a node of the mariadb group: docker exec -it mariadb mariadb -uroot -p -e \ 'SELECT DISTINCT ac.id, ac.name, ac.user_id, ac.project_id FROM keystone.application_credential ac JOIN keystone.application_credential_access_rule acar ON acar.application_credential_id = ac.internal_id;' Ask the owners to delete credentials that have been handed to parties that are not trusted with the full permissions of the owner, and to issue them again once the patched images are deployed. Requiring a service role for service tokens ahead of the update. Add the option of the fixed releases to the configuration overlays of the services that do not set it, for example for Nova: environments/kolla/files/overlays/nova.conf [keystone_authtoken] service_token_roles_required = true Do the same in neutron.conf, placement.conf, octavia.conf and in the overlays of further enabled API services, and apply the change with osism apply -a reconfigure <service>. This closes the bypass in these services; the behavior change described in the warning above applies in the same way. It does not protect the Glance API, which accepts any value in X-Service-Token because of delay_auth_decision. The bypass leaves no specific trace in the logs: the middleware logs a valid token that fails the role check as a service token only once per process, and the request itself looks like any other API call.

This section explains OSISM's architecture, the components that make up a cloud pod, and the design principles that guide technology choices.

The diagram above shows an overview of a fully open source OSISM-managed cloud pod. It illustrates the key orchestration, network, compute and storage components of it and how these interact. Each of the core components and their functions are described in the section below.

The OSISM Manager is the central control point of every OSISM deployment and the operator's single point of entry for deploying, configuring, and operating all services in a cloud pod. The entire environment is orchestrated through the osism CLI: all tasks are handed to the manager, which reads the configuration options from the local Git configuration repository and applies them with Ansible against the inventory generated from NetBox. All Ansible-based automation — for OpenStack, Ceph, infrastructure, and Kubernetes — runs through the manager's job queue system. See the OSISM Manager page for a detailed breakdown of the manager's components.

The OSISM MetalBox is a hardware-provisioning toolkit built around OpenStack Ironic that provisions both servers and switches. From the cabling and IPAM data in NetBox, the SONiC configuration is generated and pushed to the switches via ZTP, while server installation is orchestrated through the integrated Ironic using Redfish and virtual-media images. The MetalBox bundles every component required to install an OSISM environment offline — NetBox as the source of truth, an OSISM Manager, a container registry, an APT repository, and an HTTP server for the deploy images. See the OSISM MetalBox page for a detailed breakdown of the MetalBox's components.

The Git configuration repository serves as the single source of truth for the entire environment. It holds all configuration options for Kolla as well as the IPAM and cabling information that forms the basis for NetBox. Following the GitOps principle, all changes are made here first and then rolled out through the OSISM Manager or the MetalBox.

NetBox provides the cabling, the roles of the individual components, and IPAM. The local instance is populated from the configuration repository and serves as the source of information for the OSISM Manager and the MetalBox. Because NetBox provides documentation and configuration at the same time, any config drift is avoided.

The network is provided through BGP-unnumbered host-based routing. The entire configuration is generated by the MetalBox and rolled out to the switches via ZTP and to the servers through Ironic. Concepts such as MLAG, Spanning Tree, or bonding are fully replaced by BFD, BGP, and ECMP. Details about the network design can be found in the Cluster Network section.

The IaaS layer is provided by OpenStack. Underlying shared services like MariaDB, Valkey (Redis with OSISM 10 and earlier), RabbitMQ, and Memcache, as well as OpenStack itself, are provisioned via the OSISM Manager with Kolla Ansible to the respective servers. The selection and configuration of the OpenStack services happen in the Git configuration repository. The assignment of control, compute, network, and monitoring roles is controlled by NetBox.

Ceph is installed and initially configured as the open-source storage backend through the OSISM Manager. Further management, upgrades, and performance tuning are handled through cephadm. Integration with OpenStack is enabled by importing the Ceph keyrings into the Git configuration repository.

Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS) with OpenStack Software Defined Storage (SDS) with Ceph Bare Metal as a Service (BMaaS) with Ironic Software Defined Networking (SDN) with SONiC & OVN Kubernetes (K8s) with K3S Kubernetes as a Service (KaaS) with Gardener Kubernetes as a Service (KaaS) with Cluster API Identity & Access Management with Keycloak Privileged Access Management (PAM) with Teleport Logging, Monitoring & Telemetry with Prometheus & Grafana Realtime insights with Netdata

OSISM cuts one major release per year, anchored on the spring SLURP (YYYY.1) OpenStack release, and supports the current release plus the one before it. The Release Cadence chapter explains the release timing, which OpenStack releases OSISM ships, and how long each release is maintained.

OSISM integrates proven open source projects into a cohesive cloud platform. As technology evolves, OSISM adapts by evaluating and adopting new approaches while providing controlled migration paths. Read more in the Technology Adaptability chapter.
See the Cluster Layout page for recommended node counts and the impact of cluster size on quorum and data replication.
